queue.title: After a Wildfire, Clean-Looking Water May Not Be Safe
queue.description:
After a wildfire, drinking water can look clean and smell normal even when it's contaminated.

Heat-damaged plastic pipes and pressure changes can introduce chemicals such as benzene. You cannot reliably judge water safety by sight or smell.

If there's a Do Not Drink advisory, boiling does not make it safe. Follow local utility guidance and use appropriate laboratory testing.

Test before you trust.

Water-quality training: https://halowatertour.com

queue.title: Turbocor Bearing Fault: What Most Techs Blame On the Bearings
queue.description:
The Turbocor keeps tripping on bearing faults. The bearings test good, the sensors test good, and it still trips. A bearing fault reads like a bad bearing, and a bad bearing means a new compressor, so that is the call most techs make. The fault does not always mean the bearing failed.

High lift, wet suction, a weak inverter, a bad bearing calibration, and a demagnetized shaft can all trip the bearings, and only some of them mean a new compressor. This one comes out of a live stream question about a Turbocor faulting with no lift problem. It walks through each cause, why an inverter can pass every meter test and still be the problem, and what to pull from the logs before you condemn the compressor.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- Why high lift pushes a Turbocor toward surge, and how a stall that only grumbles on an oiled machine can trip a mag bearing that is perfectly fine
- The real bearing failures: a bad bearing coil or sensor
- How a weak inverter loses a stable field in the stator, lets the rotor move, and trips the bearings
- Why an inverter that passes every meter test can still be causing the faults
- Why a failed radial bearing means a new compressor, and why bearings that test good usually are good
- Shaft demag: how a demagnetized permanent magnet shaft throws off the bearings' control of the shaft orbit
- Why the inverter is the one cause that does not mean a new compressor, and when swapping in a known good one makes sense
- The five main causes to verify, and how to lay out inverter first versus new compressor for the customer
- Wet suction and carryover, through the evaporator or the economizer, as another cause of bearing faults
- How a bearing calibration check should be run, with everything else unplugged from the I/O module, and why you don't save over the factory calibration unless you have to
- Why a calibration check that shows a problem rules the inverter out
- What usually drives a shaft to demagnetize: a rotor running hot because the cooling circuit can't hold stator temp or the inverter is getting weak
- Why faults that hit after you walk away point to lift or wet suction, and how suction and discharge superheat in the logs tell the evaporator side from the economizer side
- Why a wet suction problem can show on one compressor and not the other

More chiller training: https://chilleracademy.com

queue.title: This is What Great Leaders Do
Stop Dumping Tasks Without Clear Instructions
Stop Hovering Over Staff and Avoid the Helicopter Managing Style
The Real Pain of Micromanaging
Stop Being Your Business’s Bottleneck
Heat Pump Heating Checks: Thermostat, Aux Heat, Pressures
queue.description:
When a heat pump is running in heating mode, the readings and checks look different from cooling, and that’s where a lot of techs go wrong. In this video, Bryan Orr goes through the key heat pump checks to make before and during heating season, from the thermostat to the gauges.

Thermostat configuration is the first thing to check and the most common cause of a heat pump that won’t heat. The AC runs fine all summer, then the first cold night shows a setting that was configured wrong. Bryan explains why the thermostat should be part of every maintenance visit.

Next is the reversing valve. On most systems, the reversing valve must be energized or de-energized correctly for the system to switch into heat. Hearing the valve click isn’t enough. A valve can’t actually shift without a pressure differential, so the compressor has to be running. Bryan’s practical approach: use thermostat service mode if you have it, run the system in heat for a couple of minutes, and confirm the valve really shifts.

Aux heat comes next. Auxiliary heat should run as little as possible, or customers will see high heating bills. The time it matters most is defrost, when the system switches into cooling mode and blows cold air through the house. That’s when the nuisance calls come in. Bryan explains why making sure the heat strips come on and go off matters more to him than testing defrost on every visit. He also shows his preferred test: power the W call from the outdoor unit with a simple jumper, which also confirms the white wire has continuity between the indoor and outdoor units.

Finally, heat pump pressures in heating mode. Bryan covers where to connect your gauges (the common suction port between the reversing valve and the compressor) and the number one mistake techs make. Low suction pressure in heat mode doesn’t automatically mean the system is low on charge. The colder it is outside, the lower the suction will be. 40°F outdoors in heating is like 40°F return air in cooling. High head pressure in heat mode is usually an airflow problem, not a refrigerant problem, so confirm the airflow before you blame the charge. measureQuick has a heat pump heating mode that flags these readings for you.

queue.title: Why your sink gurgles when the toilet flushes
queue.description:
Flush the toilet. Hear the sink gurgle?

Your plumbing is trying to tell you something.

Drain systems need air to work properly. When venting is blocked or the drainage system has another restriction, pressure changes can pull air through nearby traps.

That gurgling sound is a warning.

And if a trap loses its water seal, sewer gas can enter the house.

Does your sink gurgle when you flush the toilet? Tell me which fixture does it.

queue.title: The new fitting failed in a year. The old pipe is fine. Here's why.
queue.description:
The new fitting failed. The old pipe is fine. Here's why.

Put dissimilar metals together in a plumbing system, add water, and you can create conditions for galvanic corrosion.

One metal starts deteriorating faster because of its connection to the other.

It's not always a bad fitting. Sometimes it's the combination of materials.

The right transition fittings and compatible materials matter.

queue.title: Bacon grease down the drain with hot water? Here's where it ends up.
queue.description:
Hot water and dish soap. That's how you get bacon grease down the drain. Right?

That's how you get it INTO the drain.

Your pipes cool down. The grease cools, sticks to the inside, and every pan adds another layer.

Eventually, you've built a restriction you can't see.

Pour cooled grease into a container for disposal and wipe the pan before washing it.

Jar people, comment JAR.

queue.title: Tight 90 vs long sweep: one of these is a clog magnet
queue.description:
One of these fittings might be why your drain clogs in the same spot every year.

A tight 90 and a long-sweep 90 make the same turn, but they don't move waste through the pipe the same way.

Drain water carries solids. Sharp turns can create places where material collects and clogs develop.

That's why proper drainage fittings matter.

Plumbers, what's the worst fitting you've pulled out of a wall and thought, "Who installed this?"
